tagline: A freeway through farmland, past lakes and a town’s capital ambitions.
intro: I-69 runs through farmland and woodland in southern Michigan, passing Coldwater Lake and crossing the St. Joseph and Kalamazoo rivers. This four-lane stretch carries the I-69 Recreational Heritage Route from the Indiana line to the Calhoun–Eaton county line. Established in 2004, the heritage route is now a Pure Michigan Byway. Business loops connect the freeway with the downtown districts of adjacent cities.

The initial interstate plan followed a different course: a proposed link from South Bend to Kalamazoo shifted east in 1958 to connect Indianapolis with Marshall. Construction followed: Michigan’s first segment signed I-69 opened in 1967. By the end of that year it reached I-94 northwest of Marshall. US 27 shared the freeway from the state line toward Lansing until its designation was removed in 2002. At Coldwater, a business loop follows the older road into downtown.

Traveling north, the road passes Coldwater Lake before curving past Coldwater’s east side. US 12 meets the freeway immediately east of downtown Coldwater. It crosses the St. Joseph River, bypasses Tekonsha on the west and bends past Nottawa Lake. Beyond the Kalamazoo River, Marshall lies east of the freeway; the route then crosses I-94 and continues to the Eaton County boundary.

moments.title: Coldwater Lake
moments.text: Coldwater Lake feeds a river that runs north into the city of Coldwater. Channels connect it to five other lakes, reaching Quincy through East Long, Wright, Archer, Middle and Marble lakes. Although its deepest point reaches 92 feet, the lake has multiple sandbars and shallow areas. Homes occupy most of the shoreline, with more residences on Iyopawa Island in the southern part of the lake. The water covers 1,610 acres in Branch County. Downstream, the Coldwater River joins the St. Joseph River, carrying the lake’s drainage onward toward Lake Michigan.

moments.title: Tibbits Opera House, Coldwater
moments.text: Coldwater’s place on the Detroit–Chicago railway helped make it a stop for touring performers. Barton S. Tibbits, the mayor and a cigar businessman, built the opera house that opened in 1882. By the late 1950s the building was boarded up and scheduled for demolition, but local supporters raised money to save it. A later restoration returned its French Second Empire facade in 2013. The cupola is a reconstruction, hoisted into place in 2009. The Tibbits Opera Foundation and Arts Council, founded in 1963, operates the theater year-round as a community arts center.

moments.title: Marshall
moments.text: Marshall’s Governor’s Mansion began as a wager on the town’s political future. In 1839, state senator James Wright Gordon campaigned to make Marshall the capital and built a house opposite the proposed Capitol site. Gordon became acting governor in 1841, but Lansing won the capital in 1847. The house had carried its ambitious name since construction. Its white frame exterior and wide Doric portico give that ambition a visible form. In 1967, later owners’ heirs donated the property to the local Mary Marshall Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution, which converted it into a meeting hall and museum.
